title: URL shortener designed like a system design interview
summary: A URL shortener built from a written design doc, with capacity estimates, caching, rate limiting and a load test that checks the design's claims.
why: System design comes up in some internship loops and in nearly every new-grad loop. Building a classic design and measuring it lets you discuss trade-offs from experience instead of memorized diagrams.
brief:
Treat this as a system design interview that you then actually build. Start with a design doc: requirements (shorten a URL, redirect quickly, optional custom aliases and expiry, basic click counts), non-requirements, back-of-the-envelope estimates (for example, 1 million new links a month and 100 redirects per new link: how many requests per second, and how much storage over five years?), the API, the data model, how short codes are generated, and the main trade-offs.

Then build it: an API service, a relational database as the source of truth, and Redis as a cache for code-to-URL lookups. Generate short codes in a way you can defend (base62 encoding of a database ID, or random codes with collision checks) and explain the trade-off between predictability and coordination. Choose 301 or 302 redirects deliberately and write down why, given that you count clicks. Add rate limiting on link creation, validation that rejects anything but http and https URLs, and click counting that does not slow down the redirect path.

Finally, measure. Load test the redirect endpoint with and without the cache and report throughput and latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99). Your design doc's estimates plus your measurements are the showcase.

milestones.title: Design doc
tasks: Estimate requests per second, storage over five years and cache size, showing the arithmetic
Specify the API, the schema and the short-code strategy, with the alternatives you considered
milestones.doneWhen: The design doc includes estimates with their arithmetic, an architecture diagram, and a trade-offs section comparing at least two ways to generate codes.

milestones.title: Core service
tasks: A POST endpoint that creates a short link, and GET /{code} that redirects
Base62 encoding (or random codes with collision handling) with unit tests
Validate URLs and support optional custom aliases and expiry
milestones.doneWhen: Creating a link and following it works end to end, and tests cover collisions or uniqueness, invalid URLs, expired links and duplicate aliases.

milestones.title: Caching
tasks: Cache code-to-URL lookups in Redis with a TTL (cache-aside)
Invalidate or update the cache when a link is deleted or expires
milestones.doneWhen: Repeated redirects for a popular code are served from the cache, as the hit and miss counters show.

milestones.title: Rate limiting and analytics
tasks: Rate limit link creation per client, for example with a token bucket in Redis
Count clicks asynchronously (a queue or batched writes) so redirects stay fast
Add a stats endpoint for a link
milestones.doneWhen: Going over the limit returns 429 with a Retry-After header, and click counts are exact after a burst of 1,000 redirects.

milestones.title: Load test and report
tasks: Load test redirects with a tool such as k6, Locust or wrk, with the cache on and off
Record throughput and p50, p95 and p99 latency
Compare the results with your design doc's estimates
milestones.doneWhen: The README contains a results table for cache on and off and a paragraph explaining the difference.

stretch: Run two API instances behind a load balancer and show they share the cache correctly
Add a read replica and route redirect lookups to it
Expire and clean up old links with a background job
Add abuse protection, such as checking URLs against a blocklist
rubric: A reviewer should see a design doc with requirements, estimates with arithmetic, a diagram and explicit trade-offs
A reviewer should see the short-code strategy explained and tested, including collisions or uniqueness
A reviewer should see a cache-aside cache with a TTL and correct invalidation
A reviewer should see a deliberate choice of 301 or 302, with the reason written down
A reviewer should see rate limiting that returns 429 with Retry-After
A reviewer should see load test results with latency percentiles, with and without the cache
A reviewer should be able to start the system with one Docker Compose command
showcase: Put the architecture diagram and the load test results table at the top of the README
Link the design doc, including its estimates section
Add a short 'What I would change at 100 times the scale' section
Use it for system design practice: be able to sketch the whole design on a whiteboard in 30 minutes
resumeBullet: Designed and built a URL shortener (FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis) from a written design doc; a cache-aside Redis layer cut p95 redirect latency from 45 ms to 8 ms in a 1,000 requests-per-second load test.
interviewTalkingPoints: Base62 IDs versus random codes: predictability, collisions and coordination between servers
301 versus 302, and how browser caching of redirects affects click counting
Why cache-aside with a TTL, and what happens when a viral link's cache entry expires under heavy load
How you kept click counting off the redirect's critical path
How your measured numbers compared with your estimates, and why
